content: Hydroxyurea is a medication that can cause severe and potentially life-threatening side effects, including a significant reduction in blood cell counts. It is crucial to inform your doctor if you have or have ever had a blood disorder. Additionally, you should provide your doctor and pharmacist with a complete list of all medications you are currently taking. Combining hydroxyurea with other medications that lower blood cell counts may increase the severity of side effects. If you experience symptoms such as fever, sore throat, chills, cough, or other signs of infection; extreme fatigue; weakness; pale skin; dizziness; confusion; rapid heartbeat; shortness of breath; difficulty sleeping; or unusual bleeding or bruising, contact your doctor immediately. Regular appointments with your doctor and laboratory tests are essential to monitor your response to hydroxyurea and to check for any significant drops in your blood cell counts. If your blood counts become too low, your doctor may adjust your dosage or temporarily stop the medication to allow your blood counts to recover. Hydroxyurea may increase the risk of developing cancer, particularly with long-term use. Discuss the potential risks with your doctor. Women taking hydroxyurea, or whose male partners are taking it, may have reduced fertility, but pregnancy is still possible. Inform your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or if you become pregnant while taking hydroxyurea. Use reliable contraception during treatment, as hydroxyurea can harm or even be fatal to a developing fetus. Hydroxyurea is prescribed to treat various conditions, including melanoma (a type of skin cancer), chronic myelocytic leukemia (CML), recurrent or metastatic ovarian cancer, and primary squamous cell carcinoma of the head or neck (excluding the lips) when used with radiation therapy. It is also used to prevent painful crises and reduce the need for blood transfusions in individuals with sickle cell anemia. Hydroxyurea works by slowing or stopping the growth of cancer cells and altering red blood cells to prevent them from assuming an abnormal shape in sickle cell anemia. The duration of treatment depends on your condition and how your body responds to the medication. Hydroxyurea is typically taken once daily, but for certain cancers, it may be taken every third day. Take the medication at the same time each day as directed by your doctor. Do not take more or less than prescribed, and do not stop taking it without consulting your doctor. If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember, unless it is almost time for your next dose. Do not take a double dose to make up for a missed one. If you miss more than one dose, contact your doctor. Hydroxyurea may also be used to treat polycythemia vera (a condition with excessive blood cell production), psoriasis (a skin condition with red, scaly patches), and hypereosinophilic syndrome (a condition with excessive production of a specific type of white blood cell). Discuss the risks and benefits of using hydroxyurea for these conditions with your doctor. Before starting hydroxyurea, inform your doctor and pharmacist if you are allergic to it or any of its ingredients. Provide a list of all prescription and nonprescription medications, vitamins, and supplements you are taking. Certain medications, such as those for HIV/AIDS (e.g., didanosine, stavudine), probenecid, or sulfinpyrazone, may interact with hydroxyurea. Inform your doctor if you have HIV/AIDS, have undergone radiation therapy or chemotherapy, or have a history of kidney or liver disease. Breastfeeding is not recommended during treatment with hydroxyurea. Your doctor may prescribe folic acid supplements to take during treatment. Always handle hydroxyurea capsules with disposable gloves, and wash your hands before and after handling them. If the powder from a capsule spills, clean it immediately with a damp disposable towel, place the towel in a sealed container, and dispose of it in a trash can out of reach of children and pets. Hydroxyurea may cause side effects. Common minor side effects include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, and drowsiness. Serious side effects include rash, discoloration of the skin or nails, loss of sensation in specific areas, skin or mouth sores, foul-smelling discharge from the skin, and swelling of the hands, feet, ankles, or lower legs. If you experience any of these symptoms, contact your doctor immediately. Report any unusual problems to your doctor, and serious side effects can be reported to the FDA's MedWatch program. Store hydroxyurea in its original container, tightly closed, and out of reach of children and pets. Keep it at room temperature, away from heat and moisture. Dispose of outdated or unused medication properly, and consult your doctor or pharmacist for guidance. In case of overdose, contact your local poison control center at 1-800-222-1222. If the individual collapses or is not breathing, call 911. Symptoms of overdose may include violet discoloration, swelling, and soreness of the palms and soles, skin scaling, darkened skin, and mouth sores. Do not share this medication with others. Consult your pharmacist if you have questions about refilling your prescription.
